lesson.title: Added Experiences: The Positive Symptoms of Schizophrenia
lesson.summary: Positive symptoms of schizophrenia are experiences and behaviors added on top of typical functioning, including hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, and disorganized behavior, not symptoms that are in any way "good."
lesson.body:
The word "positive" in positive symptoms is one of the most commonly misunderstood terms in this whole unit, so it's worth being precise from the start. It has nothing to do with something being good. In this context, positive means added, an experience or behavior present in someone with schizophrenia that is not part of typical functioning for most people. This sits in direct contrast with negative symptoms, covered next, which describe functions that are reduced or missing.

Hallucinations are perceptual experiences that occur without an external stimulus actually causing them, and in schizophrenia they can occur in any sensory channel, though auditory hallucinations, most often described as hearing voices, are the most commonly reported type in the research literature. These voices might comment on the person's actions, hold a conversation, or issue commands, and they are experienced as genuinely real, not as an imagined or deliberate thought.

Delusions are fixed, false beliefs held with strong conviction despite clear evidence against them, and which are not better explained by the person's cultural or religious background. Several types show up commonly enough to have their own names: persecutory delusions involve a conviction that one is being watched, followed, or plotted against; grandiose delusions involve an inflated, unrealistic sense of one's own importance, power, or identity; and referential delusions involve the belief that neutral events, such as a stranger's comment or a detail on television, carry special personal meaning directed specifically at the person.

Disorganized speech and thought is another positive symptom, showing up as a loosening of the logical connections between ideas, so that speech can become tangential, hard to follow, or in more severe cases largely incoherent. Disorganized or unusual motor behavior can range from unpredictable agitation to, in some cases, catatonia, a marked decrease in responsiveness to the surrounding environment.

Positive symptoms are the ones most classically linked to overactive dopamine signaling in certain brain pathways, an idea developed in the dopamine hypothesis, and they also tend to respond relatively well to antipsychotic medications that work by blocking dopamine receptors, though response varies from person to person and this connection is more useful as a general pattern than as a precise rule. Above all, it's worth remembering that these are genuinely distressing, often frightening experiences for the person living through them. They deserve to be understood factually and treated with the same seriousness and compassion as any other medical symptom, not dismissed, sensationalized, or mocked.
